overview: NZME is New Zealand's largest multi-platform media company, publishing the NZ Herald and regional/community titles, operating a portfolio of radio brands (Newstalk ZB, ZM, Hauraki, The Hits) and digital audio via iHeartRadio, and owning the OneRoof residential property portal. Demerged from APN News & Media and dual-listed on the NZX and ASX in June 2016, NZME reports in NZD with a 31 December fiscal year end. The business is in a structural transition from a legacy print/radio advertising model toward digital subscriptions, digital audio and property-listing revenue, against a backdrop of secular print decline and a cyclical, currently subdued, NZ advertising and housing market.

business_model.summary: NZME earns revenue from three operating divisions -- Publishing, Audio and OneRoof -- through a mix of advertising (print, radio, digital display/programmatic), reader/subscriber revenue (print and digital-only news subscriptions), and property-listing fees paid by real estate agents/vendors on OneRoof. Historically an advertising-led business, NZME has pursued a 'digital-first' and increasingly subscription-led strategy: FY2025 digital revenue was over 42% of total company revenue, and management explicitly frames subscription and listings revenue as more stable and higher-quality than pure advertising income. GrabOne, a daily-deals e-commerce business, was divested in 2021 (sold for NZ$17.5m) and is no longer part of the group -- it is not a recent (2024/25) divestment as sometimes assumed.

revenue_streams.name: Publishing (NZ Herald, BusinessDesk, regional/community print, digital subscriptions & advertising)
Audio (Newstalk ZB, ZM, Hauraki, The Hits, iHeartRadio, podcasting)
revenue_streams.trend: growing (digital audio +10% YoY FY2025; terrestrial stable)

revenue_streams.name: OneRoof (property listings, digital & print real estate)
revenue_streams.trend: growing (digital listings +19% YoY FY2025; print declining -17%)

business_model.customer_type: Mixed B2C (news/audio subscribers and listeners) and B2B (advertisers, media agencies, and real estate agents/vendors on OneRoof)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand -- no meaningful international revenue exposure
business_model.revenue_quality_notes: FY2025 total operating revenue was NZ$345.1m (2024: NZ$350.2m), roughly flat to slightly down; adjusting for the December 2024 closure of 14 unprofitable community newspaper titles, continuing-business revenue was ~1% higher YoY. Publishing digital-only subscriptions grew 10% YoY to 166,000, taking total publishing subscriptions (print + digital) to over 243,000 (from 236,000). Digital subscription revenue growth (+3% in FY2025) is currently only partly offsetting declines in print subscriber and retail-outlet sales, and print advertising remains in structural decline even as digital advertising also softened in 2025 due to a deliberate pullback from low-margin third-party programmatic inventory.

main_competitors: Stuff (NZ's other major newspaper/digital publisher, owned by Sinead Boucher; also a print-plant supplier/counterparty to NZME)
Trade Me (NZ's dominant online marketplace, including Trade Me Property -- the clear #1 property portal)
Mediaworks (competing radio group -- MoreFM, The Edge, George FM etc.)
Warner Bros. Discovery / Sky NZ / TVNZ (broadcast and streaming video, competing for advertising dollars)
Google and Meta (dominant recipients of NZ digital advertising spend; also a competitive/complementary relationship via commercial news-licensing deals)
realestate.co.nz (industry-owned property listing site) and homes.co.nz (owned by Trade Me since 2021)
competitive_position.market_position: Clear #1 in New Zealand news publishing (NZ Herald) and #1 or #2 in commercial radio audience/revenue share (44.3% average audio revenue share vs Mediaworks in FY2025, on 35.9% audience share). In property listings, OneRoof is a distant #2 to Trade Me Property, which has decades of incumbency, superior traffic and, since acquiring homes.co.nz, a broadened value proposition. Stuff and Trade Me have also been reported to be cooperating/partnering in real estate, which would further pressure OneRoof's competitive position.

moat_factors.description: NZ Herald and Newstalk ZB are the most recognised news brands in the country, reaching roughly 9 in 10 Kiwis across NZME's platforms combined, which supports advertiser reach and subscriber trust.
Newstalk ZB and ZM are consistently the top-rating breakfast shows nationally; NZME holds ~44% of radio ad revenue share, giving it negotiating leverage with agencies.
NZME can bundle audio, publishing and OneRoof inventory for advertisers/agents in a way single-platform competitors cannot, cited by management as a differentiator for OneRoof specifically.

Property portals are classic winner-take-most two-sided markets; Trade Me's larger buyer audience makes it the default listing choice for agents, and OneRoof's #2 position has not translated into first-mover-type scale advantages despite years of investment.

moat_factors.factor: Regulatory/scale barriers to entry in radio and news
moat_factors.description: Broadcasting spectrum, existing newsroom infrastructure and journalist talent create real (though not insurmountable) barriers for new entrants; the Commerce Commission's 2017-18 blocking of the NZME/Fairfax merger is itself evidence regulators view NZ media concentration as a serious competition issue, implying NZME already holds meaningful market power in publishing.

weaknesses: Distant #2 (or weaker) in property listings against an entrenched Trade Me, in a category with strong winner-take-most economics
Legacy print cost base (presses, distribution, paper) remains a drag on margins even as print revenue shrinks
Heavily dependent on the small, cyclical NZ advertising market with no geographic diversification

Structurally exposed to Google/Meta's share of digital ad spend, which continues to erode publisher-direct programmatic revenue (NZME deliberately cut low-margin third-party digital marketing sales in 2025)
Small-cap scale (~NZ$150-250m market cap) limits capital available for reinvestment relative to global platform competitors

growth_drivers: OneRoof: continued listings-upgrade penetration and average-yield growth (residential listings revenue +19% YoY in FY2025); a new OneRoof app (early 2026) and in-housing of technology development aimed at faster product iteration; potential value realisation via the ongoing strategic review

Digital audio and podcasting: digital audio revenue +10% YoY in FY2025, with podcasts now over 30% of digital audio revenue; new formats (iHeartCountry NZ launch, upgraded iHeartRadio app) aimed at growing share of a structurally growing digital-audio ad market

Digital subscriptions in Publishing: digital-only subscribers +10% YoY to 166,000; new products (Herald NOW video streaming, a new NZ Herald mobile app, BusinessDesk re-platforming) intended to lift subscriber lifetime value and reduce reliance on advertising

Cost-out program: NZ$12m of annualised cost savings completed in 2025 (fully realised in 2026, delivering a further ~NZ$3m improvement) via a simplified three-division operating structure (Publishing, Audio, OneRoof)

Potential cyclical recovery: management guided Q1-2026 advertising revenue tracking towards +3% YoY growth led by audio, and struck a 'cautiously optimistic' tone on a gradual 2026 economic recovery, though this softened somewhat into January 2026

Possible Google/Meta commercial revenue growth: existing multi-year commercial licensing deals with Google (News Showcase, finalised 2022) and Meta provide an incremental, largely fixed revenue stream independent of a Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill

Optionality from consolidation: renewed (though currently paused) discussions with Stuff around asset acquisitions (Petone print-plant equipment deal completed; broader masthead/OneRoof-accelerating discussions paused in March 2025 pending board outcome) could resurface now the board is settled

business.description: Print advertising and subscriber/retail sales continue to decline (publishing total reader revenue -3% YoY in FY2025); digital growth is not yet fully offsetting this on a like-for-like basis, and the mix shift pressures margins given largely fixed print production and distribution costs.

OneRoof remains a clear #2 to Trade Me Property; reports of Stuff and Trade Me coordinating in real estate would further entrench the incumbent. If OneRoof cannot close the audience/listings gap, the 'option value' thesis behind the strategic review may not be realised.

business.risk: Advertiser dependence on a small, single-country market
business.description: 100% NZ revenue base with no geographic diversification; NZME's fortunes are tied entirely to NZ business and consumer confidence.
Brand strength in radio (Mike Hosking, Fletch Vaughan & Hayley) and publishing is talent-dependent; NZME flagged senior OneRoof leadership turnover during 2025 as a live issue.

Multiple leadership and organisational-structure changes in 2025 (new CFO, new Chief of OneRoof, unified publishing structure, new sales divisions) create integration and continuity risk even as they aim to improve accountability.

financial.description: Net debt was NZ$15.5m at FY2025-end (down from $24.1m), leverage below the 0.5-1.0x EBITDA target range -- balance sheet is currently conservative, but net debt rose to $33.3m at H1-2025 (partly dividend timing), showing some intra-year variability.

Dividend policy targets 50-80% of free cash flow (raised from 30-50% in 2022); FY2025 payout ratio was 67% of a $25.4m FCF base. FCF is capex-light currently (FY2025 capex $10.7m, below FY2024's elevated digital-product spend) but a legacy print business still requires periodic press/distribution capex, and FCF itself is a function of a currently improving but still-below-mid-cycle advertising market.

NZME has repeatedly taken large non-cash goodwill/masthead impairments (e.g., $24.0m in FY2024), driving statutory NPAT to a loss in years when underlying cash generation was positive. Statutory NPAT swung from a $16.0m loss (FY2024, impairment-driven) to $13.1m profit (FY2025); investors should focus on Operating EBITDA ($62.3m FY2025, +15% YoY), Operating NPAT ($17.7m) and free cash flow ($25.4m) as the more representative measures of underlying performance, while recognising further impairments remain possible given still-depressed asset values in legacy print/masthead intangibles.

regulatory.risk: Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill in limbo
regulatory.description: The Bill, which would have required Google/Meta to negotiate payment for NZ news content, was put on hold by the Government in December 2024 after Australia's own toughened-legislation plans stalled amid US tariff-threat pressure. As of mid-2026 there has been no revival and the Minister for Media and Communications says no decisions have been made. If never passed, NZME forgoes a potential incremental, mandated revenue stream; if passed, Google has previously threatened (as in Canada/Australia precedents) to reduce or remove news links/products in response, which is a tail risk to referral traffic and to the existing voluntary commercial deals.

regulatory.risk: Existing Google/Meta commercial deals: renewal uncertainty
regulatory.description: NZME's Google News Showcase deal was a five-year agreement finalised in 2022 (implying renewal due around 2027), alongside a separate Meta subscriber-growth funding deal from 2022. These voluntary deals were reported to be worth roughly $2.5-5m per annum in incremental value collectively for NZME (with other NZ publishers); no confirmation was found in available sources of 2025/2026 renewal terms, and platform-side willingness to continue funding news in the absence of binding legislation is a genuine risk (Meta has walked away from equivalent deals/programs in other markets).

The Commerce Commission's 2017-18 rejection (upheld on appeal) of the NZME/Fairfax merger establishes a clear precedent that any large-scale NZME/Stuff combination would face serious competition-law scrutiny, constraining the most obvious consolidation path even though the underlying economic case (shared cost base, reduced duplicate newsrooms) remains attractive to both parties.

macro.description: Advertising revenue is highly correlated with NZ GDP growth and business/consumer confidence; NZME explicitly cites a 'prolonged economic slowdown' through 2025 and only a 'gradual' expected recovery in 2026, with January 2026 activity softening after a weaker-than-expected December.

OneRoof's revenue is directly levered to national residential listing volumes, which per REINZ/Tony Alexander data referenced in the FY2025 annual report remain below the 2007-2024 historical average. A weak housing cycle caps OneRoof's near-term growth and value-realisation prospects regardless of product execution.

NZ mortgage rates and RBNZ policy directly influence both housing transaction volumes (OneRoof) and broader consumer/business confidence (advertising); a slower-than-expected rate-cutting cycle would prolong the current soft patch.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand traditional media advertising continues to shrink structurally as spend migrates to Google/Meta and digital-native channels; audio (radio + digital audio/podcasting) has proven more resilient than print, and property/classifieds has consolidated into a small number of digital portals. NZME's own commentary frames 2025 as a 'challenging economic climate' with a 'gradual recovery' expected through 2026.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High -- advertising and property-listing revenue are both classic late-cycle discretionary spend categories; NZME's earnings swing materially with the NZ economic and housing cycle.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high indirect sensitivity via mortgage rates/housing turnover (OneRoof) and business/consumer confidence (advertising); low direct sensitivity given modest net debt.

recent_developments.event: FY2024 results released with a statutory net loss of $16.0m (including a $24.0m intangible impairment); NZME simultaneously announced a strategic review of OneRoof (engaging Jarden) to explore separation/external capital-raising options to 'surface value' not reflected in the share price, with an update promised at the H1-2025 result.

Canadian investor Jim Grenon (via JTG 4 Limited), having built a significant NZME shareholding, publicly proposed wholesale changes to the NZME board. In response, Stuff paused the acquisition/asset discussions it had been having with NZME since late 2024, pending clarity on the board's composition.
A months-long, sometimes acrimonious board dispute played out, including a Takeovers Panel review that cleared Grenon of any Takeovers Code breach, before a negotiated compromise was reached.

At NZME's Annual Shareholders' Meeting, shareholders elected Steven Joyce (former National Party Cabinet minister) and Jim Grenon to the board; Joyce was subsequently elected Chairman. Bowen Pan (ex-Facebook Marketplace founder) was later appointed as an additional director by the board. Former Chair Barbara Chapman and director David Gibson stepped down. Bowen Pan was made chair of a newly formalised 'OneRoof Advisory Board' reporting to the main board, signalling continued strategic focus on OneRoof.

H1-2025 results: operating revenue $165.7m (down 3% YoY), Operating EBITDA $23.9m (up from $21.4m), statutory net loss of $0.4m (including $5.2m non-recurring costs, partly related to the contested AGM), free cash flow $2.2m. OneRoof residential listings revenue +16% YoY, digital revenue +22% YoY. No definitive OneRoof separation decision was announced at this result -- management said the priority remained organic value creation.

NZME agreed to acquire the print-plant equipment at Stuff's Petone facility (up to $15m investment) to bolster the economics of its own print operations, a more limited outcome than the broader Stuff asset/masthead discussions that had been paused in March.

FY2025 full-year results released: operating revenue $345.1m (-1% YoY, +1% like-for-like), Operating EBITDA $62.3m (+15% YoY), Operating NPAT $17.7m (operating EPS 9.4cps vs 6.5cps), statutory NPAT $13.1m (vs $16.0m loss in FY2024), free cash flow $25.4m, net debt down to $15.5m. Total dividends of 9.0 cps declared, flat vs FY2024, a 67% payout ratio. Management guided Q1-2026 advertising revenue tracking to roughly +3% YoY growth led by audio, but noted a softer-than-expected December 2025 and some pullback in January 2026. No formal FY2026 EBITDA guidance was given. New CFO Jo Hempstead (ex-Warehouse Group) joined in early 2026.

NZME is scheduled to release its H1-2026 (six months to 30 June 2026) results and host an investor webcast two days after this analysis was prepared (2026-08-23). This result was not yet available and is not reflected in the figures above; it should be checked directly once published for the latest read on the advertising recovery, OneRoof strategic-review progress, and any updated capital-management or dividend commentary.

items.notes: Management noted this softened slightly in January 2026 after a weaker-than-expected December 2025, though confidence in a gradual improvement through the year was maintained.

items.target: Further ~$3m improvement in 2026 from the full-year realisation of $12m annualised savings completed in 2025
items.notes: No separate new cost-out target announced beyond finishing the flow-through of 2025 initiatives; management said it will 'continue to proactively manage our cost structure.'

Management described itself as 'cautiously optimistic' for 2026 but explicitly did not issue formal EBITDA guidance; outlook language emphasised a 'gradual recovery' as inflationary pressure and global economic uncertainty linger.

items.target: 50-80% of free cash flow, subject to remaining within 0.5-1.0x EBITDA target leverage
items.notes: FY2025 payout ratio was 67%, within policy; FY2025 total dividend held flat at 9.0 cps vs FY2024.

items.target: No formal separation/monetisation decision announced; all options said to remain under consideration
items.notes: As of the FY2025 result, management's language shifted toward 'realising the full value potential of OneRoof' organically, with a new app, in-housed technology development, and continued oversight via the OneRoof Advisory Board (chaired by director Bowen Pan) rather than a confirmed spin-off/sale. Investors should watch the H1-2026 result (25 Aug 2026) for any update.

guidance.management_commentary: Chairman Steven Joyce and CEO Michael Boggs jointly stated they are 'cautiously optimistic heading into 2026,' citing improving activity levels and market sentiment but a still-gradual recovery given lingering inflation and global economic uncertainty. Three stated 2026 priorities: (1) realising the full value potential of OneRoof, (2) maintaining strong governance and operational discipline following the 2025 board renewal, and (3) adapting the cost base to preserve profitability while positioning to capture market share as conditions improve.

bull_case: Digital transition metrics are moving in the right direction across all three divisions -- digital subscriptions +10%, digital audio revenue +10%, OneRoof digital listings revenue +19% -- with digital now over 42% of total revenue, supporting a slow but real shift to a higher-quality, less cyclical revenue mix

Governance overhang has been resolved: the 2025 board dispute concluded with a negotiated settlement (Steven Joyce as Chair, Jim Grenon and Bowen Pan as directors) rather than a prolonged fight, removing a source of cost/distraction (legal and consulting costs tied to the contested AGM were a specific drag on H1-2025 statutory earnings) and installing directors with direct digital-marketplace and turnaround experience

OneRoof retains real optionality: even as a #2 portal, continued double-digit listings-revenue growth, a February-2025-initiated strategic review (Jarden-advised) exploring separation/external capital, and a dedicated OneRoof Advisory Board all point to potential value crystallisation if management can either accelerate organic growth or execute a partial monetisation

Balance sheet is currently conservative (net debt of $15.5m, leverage below the 0.5-1.0x target range) giving flexibility for further cost discipline, bolt-on M&A (e.g., further Stuff asset deals), or increased capital returns, while the FY2025 dividend (9.0 cps, ~67% payout) offers a high running yield on a beaten-down share price

Cyclical trough dynamics: NZ advertising and housing markets are described by management and independent data (REINZ/Tony Alexander listings series) as below long-run average, so a normalisation of NZ business/consumer confidence and interest rates would flow disproportionately to NZME's operating leverage (evidenced by the 15% EBITDA growth on roughly flat revenue in FY2025 through cost discipline alone)
bear_case: OneRoof's competitive position looks structurally weak: Trade Me Property remains the dominant #1 portal with superior audience scale, homes.co.nz now under Trade Me ownership, and reports of Stuff/Trade Me cooperation in real estate would further entrench the incumbent -- classic winner-take-most portal economics historically favour scale leaders, and years of NZME investment have not closed the gap

Print decline is not fully offset: publishing total reader revenue fell 3% YoY in FY2025 and digital advertising itself also declined (-7% headline, -1% core) as the low-margin third-party program was deliberately wound down -- the digital growth story is real but currently insufficient to make total publishing revenue grow

The Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, the clearest potential incremental revenue catalyst, has been shelved by the Government since December 2024 with no confirmed revival as of mid-2026, and existing Google/Meta commercial deals (originally signed 2022) face renewal uncertainty with no confirmed 2025/26 terms found in available sources -- the regulatory upside case is speculative, not scheduled

Governance renewal carries real integration/consistency risk: three new directors (including an activist investor) joined within months of each other, alongside a new CFO and reshuffled OneRoof/publishing leadership -- multiple simultaneous leadership transitions raise execution risk even if the underlying strategic direction is sound

Statutory earnings have been repeatedly distorted by large non-cash impairments ($24.0m in FY2024 alone), reflecting genuinely impaired economics in parts of the legacy print/masthead asset base; a small-cap, single-country, structurally-declining-in-parts media business trading at a modest market cap (~NZ$150-250m) offers limited liquidity and no geographic diversification to cushion a renewed domestic downturn or a further leg down in print
